utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bekavac. I'd like to thank you for coming to the Tribunal and responding to our request. For the record, would you please give us your name and surname, your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: My name is Zvonimir Bekavac. I was born on the 2nd of January, 1943, in Vitez. I am married and the father of two children. I am an engineer of the work process or organisation of work. I'm retired, and I live in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bekavac, you have spent your whole life in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How long have you worked in the company, that is, within the frameworks of the company that we tend to refer to as the SPS?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I worked there for approximately 30 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While we're on that subject, Mr. Kovacic, sometimes a company is referred to as Vitezit and sometimes the SPS. It might be helpful if we got the relationship right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That was exactly, Your Honour, what I intended, because finally we have a witness who's been there 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bekavac, could you in a few sentences explain to the Trial Chamber the organisational structure of these companies? One companies, five companies, three companies. Could you explain all the companies belonging to the same factory that were in that locality? And what is most important, could you focus on 1992 when the factory actually stopped producing.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: By the decree of the then government, that is to say, the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in 1950 a company was established which was called 202. That was its code. That coded company, 202, was later to take the name of Slobodan Princip Seljo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. The general abbreviation of that Slobodan Princip Seljo is SPS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes. That SPS company produced powders, gunpowders, for the purposes of the Yugoslav People's Army, primarily. Immediately after the founding of that SPS company, the explosives production plant was set up and the fuses plant. That was for the economy. Later on in 1965, or around 1965, this company, the SPS company, underwent a transformation, that is to say, up until its association and pooling into a business concern called Unis-Sarajevo. After that, there were a number of transformations so that when the SPS became part of Unis-Sarajevo, with several other companies, when it merged - they were also companies which produced finished products for the Yugoslav People's Army - another transformation took place in the Vitez locality. Two more firms were established. They were called Vitezit, that was one, for the production of explosives and fuses once again; and Sintevit, that was the other one, which produced plastics, chemical products mostly. These three firms coexisted until 1993. In the meantime, let me just add, these firms from Vitez became separate from Unis on the basis of a referendum. The circumstances and reasons for this were different; they were of an economic and financial nature - I don't want to tire you with that - because we felt, and many felt within the frameworks of Unis, that resources were ebbing off to Sarajevo, and the workers did not want to see their resources and funds siphoned off to Sarajevo. In view of the fact that the SPS, after the Washington Accords, or after Dayton in fact, ceased to function because of the upsets that had taken place on the market itself, it was only the explosives factory that functioned. And it produces products today and is now called the Vitezit. That's all that remains of those companies today. So that whole locality, that whole area is called Vitezit. That would briefly be the history of those companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Maybe I could ask you another few questions to clarify certain points. You mentioned that there was a referendum, and the decision taken at that referendum, on the basis of a workers' meeting and workers' votes, you decided to step down from Unis. When was that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I think that that was -- I can't tell you the exact date, but it was quite certainly four or five years before the conflicts broke out. I think that's how I would date it. I can't tell you the exact date, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But at any rate, it was in the late 1980s; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, that decision, was it in keeping with the legal system of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, because it expressed the will of the workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me also explain for the purposes of the Trial Chamber once more, the factory was what we used to call socially owned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the third point that I wanted to clarify in this connection, is it true that in the vernacular, in the popular terms that the inhabitants used, that locality, because of the factory, was called SPS or Vitezit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: It was usually called SPS because SPS was the matrix firm, the first company to be set up in 1950, so that's what they called it mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And to round off that area, we have a map for you which was -- that is to say, a map here was shown earlier on. Could you tell us with respect to territory and surface area, the surface area that the factory was over if you look at it -- the centre of Vitez. Is it a large surface area, a smaller area?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Well, I think it is larger than the centre of town. It covers a larger area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Over the last 20 years, Vitezit -- oh, I beg your pardon, let me say the SPS supplied the largest number of jobs?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, they had the largest number of employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How many employees in the area were there when it was at its peak?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Between 2.000 and 3.000. 2.000 and 3.000; the numbers would change but it was between 2.000 and 3.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the ethnic structure of the workers in that factory?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: The ethnic composition of the workers in the factory were similar to the ethnic composition of the population of Vitez municipality itself, and there are population census which will bear that out but I say that is quite certainly the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In 1992, was this ethnic composition upset in any way? Did any group leave the area?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I think until the outbreak of the conflict in 1993, I would say that everything was normal in the factory, although there were tensions because tensions existed in Vitez municipality and they did especially in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but production went on until the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The factory's leadership, management, did it assume any official policy or position when the multiparty system started up and when people came politicised, so to speak, when they took part in politics more? So what about the political life of the environment?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Well, the factory's management assumed the position that politics should have nothing to do with production and I think that, to a large extent, this was realised in practice because the production of nitroglycerin, for example, as I'm sure the Court knows, is one of the most dangerous products to produce in the world. So they did not allow politics to meddle in factory matters because it would be highly dangerous and detrimental. This is borne out by the fact that under such difficult conditions in the factory, we had no upsets, no dangerous situations, accidents or anything of that kind which did happen 10, 15, 20 years ago. There were a number of casualties in the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bekavac, did you ever happen to hear or see the factory management, in the course of 1992, give the workers an oath of loyalty to sign to the HVO, anything of that kind, a paper of that kind?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: No, I never saw that, nothing of that kind. It quite certainly did not exist, at least not in the factory. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1992 and especially at the start of 1993, the factory lost its markets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Well, the factory did lose its customary markets because Serbia, for example, was a large market. But there were other markets, some other markets in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for example. And those buyers, those markets were -- looked like a tiger's skin. They were patchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollections, could you tell us who your main buyers were, your principal buyers were in 1992, the latter half of 1992 is what we're interested in mostly.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Well, and I'm talking about the war days, as the war had already started in Bosnia-Herzegovina, our products went to markets where there was transport, where transport enabled the products to be taken. And I know that the goods, that is to say, the gunpowders, the explosives went to Tuzla, Tesanj, Visoko, Bugojno, Hrasnica, Sarajevo, and so on. So those are the localities which were under the control of the BH army and Vitez for the purpose of Vitez's defence, so this was under army control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document now. May the witness be shown a Kupreskic document which gives a breakdown of the finished products of the factory. Mr. Bekavac, the usher will show you a document. Will you please look at it. I'm sure you won't know, be able to tell us the dates and the quantities produced, but could you tell us roughly whether that represents a cross-section of what the factory produced, to the best of your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be document D113/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I should like to draw your attention, to save time, to column one, the left-hand side where the locations are stated, and everything on the right are specifications, that is to say, quantities, prices and so on. Looking at the locations, and you mentioned some of them, were those the places that the shipments went to in the period that this document says, that is to say, from May to December?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Some of these places have been listed and I think this is quite in order and quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Am I going too fast? I'll slow down a bit. Thank you. According to your recollection, when you look at these places, is it true that these were the places -- that in these places, there were various armies; the BH army in some of them and HVO in others?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Visoko, the army of B and H; Tomislavgrad and Vitez, HVO and the BiH army; Novi Travnik also HVO and the BiH; then BiH, Travnik the same. Tuzla, that was mostly the BH army. Bugojno also the BH army, HVO. Konjic, the BH army; Zavidovici, the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Teslic is now in Republika Srpska now, as far as I know. I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that you delivered goods to everyone who was able to pay for them and organise the taking over of the goods?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: That is correct. That was the biggest problem. Taking delivery was an even bigger problem than payments, but these two things are correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will come back to the ethnic composition but let us now stick to questions of production. When, in fact, as far as you remember, was there a considerable decrease in the amount of goods produced?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Well, the capacity was considerably reduced at the beginning of the Serbian aggression in Bosnia and Herzegovina because that was when the roads leading to Serbia were cut off, and that was when there was a decline which rapidly continued. And then, more or less, we had the market of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in 1993 there was a market in Croatia as well. But this was after the aggression, because most of the JNA was on the side of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I understand from this that in 1993 you made some deliveries.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1993, some deliveries of smaller quantities of goods were made, but there was a big problem of transport. Some small amounts were delivered, I know because I worked in production, and to whom these goods went exactly and in what quantities, that was the responsibility of the commercial department. I didn't have much to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You told us what goods the factory produced. Would you tell me whether there was a product that could be described as a final product, for example, a shell either for a gun or something else, something that could be used as it was?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: No. SPS mostly produced gun powders which were then used -- I would like to draw the Court's attention to this -- but the Court probably knows this, gun powder is the fuel, the nucleus of every system, the core of every system. This factory was the only one in the former Yugoslavia and one of the better and more up-to-date plants producing this in the Balkans, but this factory did not produce any final products. It only produced half-finished products which were then built into products in other military factories.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina within the former Yugoslav Federation, there was a technological chain, there were a number of factories which produced different parts, ammunition and the materiel, and together they produced something that was a single whole?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As someone who spent about 30 years in this business, could you give us some examples of part of this chain, using your job for example.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, more or less the entire military industry of the former Yugoslavia, for strategic reasons, was in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We needn't go into why this was so. But in order to complete a final product, there were several factories. As we said, the SPS produced gun powder, the metal parts were produced in Pretis, Vogosce, those were shell casings, shells and so on. The fuses were produced in Bugojno. Another part was produced in Pobjeda Gorazde. Ammunition for rifles was produced in Konjic Igman, and artillery pieces by Bratsvo Novi Travnik. And this was a whole chain without which anyone could do anything, so the whole chain had to participate in the completion of a final product.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the problems that started with greater intensity in 1992, as you said, at that time, in agreement with the buyers, was anything done in the SPS to make your product into a final product?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Because in the Vitez municipality there were no conflicts, there was no hint of a conflict yet, through various channels particular products, metal products and other auxiliary material, were brought into Vitez where they were assembled and delivered both to the army of BH and to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. To go back to the question of the ethnic makeup of the work force in the plant, was the ethnic makeup of the management of the company in the SPS location the same? In other words, did it reflect the ethnic makeup of the population of the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that was certainly true, because as far as politics was concerned, it was the League of Communists that held power until 1992/1993 and they would always intervene. They would not allow anything different to happen, so this always happened, everything had to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it was both at the level of the work force and the management.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But special attention was paid to the management level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Among your colleagues in the factory, did you have any friends whom you associated with in your spare time?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course. That was quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you mention anyone who was a neighbour or a friend and also a colleague in the factory?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: One of the managers who also held political posts in the municipality and was involved in all the economic -- all the business part in the factory was Hasan --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last name.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: -- and he was my next-door neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was he also a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a friend of mine. Before the war, we celebrated the New Year in Dubrovnik for seven or eight years running.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: For the record, would you repeat the last name.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: [redacted] He was a graduate in economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we can go on to other topics. Did you have a holiday home, a holiday house?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I had a small house on the mountain of Zabrdze, overlooking Vitez, some seven or eight kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was it there on its own, or was it a small weekend settlement?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Well, it was a small settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was there a hostel there for hikers?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In 1992, did you continue going to your weekend house?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: We did, but it was not so safe then so we went very rarely. We did go in the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: During that year, was there looting? Were these weekend houses broken into, devastated?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, there was looting because it was uninhabited. Hardly anyone lived there. It was just used for holidays and weekends. My weekend house was broken into twice and quite a lot of valuable things were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You, the owners of these houses, did you try to do something to protect your property?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes. We would gather there on Saturdays and Sundays and we used to discuss what should be done, because we regretted the situation. We had worked very hard to build these houses. They were very modest houses. Then we heard of an idea, and at first we thought we could take turns guarding it. We even employed some hunters and asked them to guard Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. our property and we would pay them. But then we heard that the HVO staff was looking through the municipality of Vitez for a place to train their soldiers. Because those were local people, many of them had not yet done their army service, so they needed training for defence against the Serbian aggression, because there was already fighting on Mount Vlasic. My son went there two or three times, below Mount Vlasic. And we supported this idea. Later on, this was actually implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Why did you support this idea? What benefit did you see in it for yourselves?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Well, the benefit we saw for ourselves was that our property would be protected, and that's how it was. Because on one occasion, the soldiers caught, in the vicinity of my weekend house, someone who was trying to break into the next-door weekend house. It was a young man from Kruscica. Then a police commission came and drew up a record, and I think a criminal report was lodged against him. That was good for us, as far as we were concerned, because there were Muslims and Croats and Serbs who had weekend houses there. But it was safer for us to go there then, it was quite safe then, so I went up there a few times, and I saw that all that was going on there was the training of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know from before the war a person called Marko Lujic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Of course. I was his boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was he by profession?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: He completed school for a qualified worker in the chemical industry; then I think he went to secondary school. He was a pyrotechnician, that was his job. He was responsible for elaboration at the test laboratory, at the pilot plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he had any artillery training? Was he able to use artillery weapons on his own, by himself?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When wartime production was organised, you were there in the factory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Who was then appointed the manager of the wartime production?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: It was Marko Lujic, and it was the defence office of the Vitez municipality, I think, that appointed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that later on during that summer the management of the factory was taken over by the defence administration of the HVO for the sake of regional interests? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well. It's correct. Marko Lujic then had a superior to whom he was responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But he remained at the factory.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was in charge of the wartime production, and the other one was in charge of the broader region. I think it was Puljici, if I remember rightly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you explain, Mr. Bekavac, what Marko Lujic did. You describe him as a pyrotechnician, according to the translation we have. I don't know what that is. Pyrotechnics means something to do with fireworks, but no doubt that isn't what was meant. Can you tell us what Mr. Lujic's job was in the factory, please.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We had in the company a testing polygon, a place for testing our products. Gunpowder is a very sensitive material and it must not leave the factory before it is tested, before it was tested at our testing plant. That was a firing range. To clarify this, at the firing range there are tables for tests resembling those where pilots are trained on the ground. It's a kind of booth where this is simulated, and we, by simulation, tested our products. Because we were working with gunpowder, which is inflammable and so on, and it is combustible and burns very fast, in the terminology we used, the people handling gunpowder during testing - these are not highly complex tasks - we used to refer to those people as pyrotechnicians, because they were technicians and this material burns and the effect resembles that of fireworks. Marko Lujic started working as an ordinary worker doing the simplest tasks, and in time he became a kind of shift leader responsible for that job and he supervised others. That was what he did up until 1993. So he was responsible for a group of people working with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bekavac, do you know anything about what Lujic did in 1992 and 1993 outside the factory, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Oh, you know, I don't really know such things. They were involved in some purchases of materiel which they needed from Gorazde, the caps. They were very difficult to get. And I'm afraid to really say something wrong, so I'd rather not answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm now ready to go on to another subject, and since there are very sensitive issues for the witness, being where he was living, I mean concerning the location, I would like to ask for a closed session because the witness said that he would under no way mention some units or persons in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Mr. Bekavac. If you need to mention any other names, or anything that you do not want said in open session, you can draw our attention to that. But I don't think we shall be getting into areas like that now. Is it true that your mother had partially moved to the [redacted] houses? Why?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Well, I suggested she did that. But she's no longer alive. I must say that she was a very courageous woman. She showed the first initiative, she said, "I'm go to sleep at their house so that if anybody were to come or anything would happen, I could protect them." She went to our next-door neighbours and spent some time there. She was there at night; she didn't stay during the day but she would sleep there at night. And I think she contributed to their protection, largely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Who was she there to protect?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: She was there to protect my neighbours, first and foremost, from these extremist groups and individuals who were out of anybody's control. Nobody controlled them. The people from Rijeka were looking after their homes, they were between the ages of 30 and 70, and not a hair on their head was harmed. But there were various groups going about. I know that one of my neighbours had a food store, and as soon as the war started, some several days later some people whom he didn't know either turned up, some special units or something of that kind - everybody would proclaim himself to be a unit - and they took off all his beer, food, sausages, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did [redacted] leave Rijeka at one point, and when did that happen if he did?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, and it's rather a touching episode. I must say it was very honest of [redacted]. I think it was the middle of June, he came to my front door and said, "Neighbour, I have decided to leave with my family and go to Zenica." He said, "I'm going mostly because I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. can see that you too are in danger. They know that you're protecting me. So I'm going because of you. Thank you for everything you've done for me." I gave him 100 Deutschemarks, and I said, "Here, have some money until you can find your way."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now one final question for you. He returned to his house after the war, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And he lives there today, does he?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned your neighbour who had the food store, a retail trade. Was that Mr. Vlado Baskarad?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the father, and his son was Anto Baskarad; that is to say, he was the nominal owner, proprietor, but I don't know whether he was still alive at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, let's make this clear for the Court. Was he a Croat, ethnically speaking?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to meet Cerkez in Rijeka afterwards?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I met Cerkez a couple of times in Rijeka. He would come to the forestry administration. After the conflict, a sort of command cadre was being formed to set up the defence, and I think we met on several occasions. Because my house and yard borders on the forestry compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On these occasions, did Cerkez ask you to do anything special?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: We would stand around, chatting. We knew each other; we had worked in the factory. Our conduct was always proper, our relations were always proper, and we knew each other from the factory. We would often talk about the situation. He was worried too about what was happening, he was surprised. Everything with respect to the Croatian side was more or less unorganised. We were afraid for ourselves and our families. On one occasion, and I remember it very well, we were standing at the steps to the forestry administration building and he said, "Zvonko, please, to avoid having any problems, you're a serious man, talk to some people at Rijeka. And all the Muslims that have stayed on, try and protect them. Don't allow some idiot to make problems." This was a moral responsibility on my part and gave me moral support. So that later on I talked to my mother and, via some other friends of mine down there, I was able to protect the people who had stayed on, right up until the middle of June. Some of them stayed on longer; some of them stayed on permanently. So that none of those people in my immediate vicinity were either killed or wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bekavac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Bekavac, when are we talking about? When was this conversation with Mr. Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: That conversation with Mr. Cerkez took place sometime between the 16th and 1st of May, that is to say, the 16th of May and the 1st of April, in that fortnight when it was most critical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You seem to have misspoken somewhere.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I said the 16th of March. The 16th of March. Is it the 16th of March? I think the conflict -- the 16th of April, I see. I misspoke. I'm sorry. That's a slip of the tongue. Between the 16th of April and the 1st of May, thereabouts; that is to say, the time when control had not yet been established over all those matters, nothing had -- there was no control. And I'm talking about the Rijeka area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, you don't remember the actual date but you do remember --

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Well, I think it was the first 15 or 20 days. The first 15 or 20 days. I never remember dates. I'm not good at dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now one final question. You said you knew Cerkez and that you worked in the factory, that he lived close to you. As the crow flies, how far from your house to Mario's house?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: As the crow flies, from my house to Mario's house, about 200, 250 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see him socially before?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Many times in the factory, and the nature of our work was such that we would often cooperate. We cooperated frequently, and we were frequently together. Mario was a mountaineer, he liked going mountaineering, and we went to Zabrdze, to the mountaineering hut there. We would see each other in mixed company, and we had a good time together on these occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let us just go back to one point, Mr. Bekavac. I'm not quite sure whether that was clear enough. The discussion you had, the conversation you had with Mario Cerkez that you recounted to us, could you tell us in what capacity -- that is to say, what was the characteristic of that communication? Did Mario address you as a commander, in his capacity as commander, or was one man speaking to another, chatting to another?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I think that it was a man-to-man talk. Although he was a commander, I don't differentiate, I don't make the difference between the two. But what is important for me was that it was his desire to protect people, and that was the most important thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bekavac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder if we can just deal with the factory first. If I haven't asked the registrar to get out Z2160 or D88.2, can I put mine on the ELMO to save time. Thank you

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This plan shows the factory, as we can see it there on the left-hand side, and indeed as you've told us, the factory area is as big as or larger than Vitez. Can you help us with this, please: Acid of one kind or another would play a part in the manufacturing process.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The witness is having a problem with his sight. It's probably better to tell him that he can look directly on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Back to the question. Acid of one kind or another plays a part in the manufacturing process.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For example, at the midpoint of April 1993 there would be very large reserves of acid in that factory.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: There were, but I wouldn't say they were very large. I have no information as to that. But I'm sure that there was some acid, yes. Because that is not my field of expertise. That was the production of nitroglycerin, and that was another area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When we're talking of reserves of acid, we're talking about tonnes of acid.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Well, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And there would also be quantities of fuel as reserves or for other purposes in the factory.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Well, there was a warehouse for transport and fuel reserves, but I don't know how much of that existed. It's a large compound, and I really can't tell you anything more. How much there was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Are you able to help us, just very generally, by pointing out where the acid reserves and where the fuel reserves were located? If you use the pointer and point it out, we'll then describe that in some way, if you can.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: This is so minutely drawn that I find it difficult to find my way round it; although I'm an expert in the factory layout, I know it well. The acid plant was in the upper part of the factory, towards Mount Zabrdze. What's all this here? I can't quite make it out --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you're having trouble --

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: -- but it would be in this area here. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And the petroleum --

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: This is a very small scale. That was at the entrance to the factory, the petroleum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. So the acid store --

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Round about here. The fuel was separate. The acid reserves and the petroleum reserves were about a kilometre away, about 1.000 metres from each other. They were at a distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the acid reserves, certainly, were down towards the end of the factory complex, quite near to Donja Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: No, no, the upper part. The upper part of the complex, not the lower part. Acid was in the upper part, towards Zabrdze. That's where it was, next to the nitroglycerin part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we've seen where he's marked it on the map. Thank you very much. The second thing about the factory is this -- you want to add something, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I don't know. This map here, I don't know. The scale is very small, too small. I'll tell you everything, I'll explain to you where it was, and then you can check it out. But the scale of this map is too minute for me to be able to show you properly. And it doesn't say anything. For example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Now, unless anything really turns on this, I think we've spent long enough on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the factory, we've heard from another witness to the effect that by the 15th of December of 1992 there was barely any work anymore at the Vitezit factory, that it had stopped because of a shortage of raw materials, and that 90 per cent of the workers had been sent home; would you agree with that description?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I said that in 1992, that is, from the beginning of the Serbian aggression, production rapidly fell. In 1992 there was a little production but to a lesser extent. In 1993 the finished products, as I said, as I told the lawyer, elements in different ways were withdrawn and distributed according to the list that I was shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've spoken about whether Muslims were losing their jobs under pressure because they were Muslims. This is a very large factory with many areas within it. You're not in a position to speak for what happened in every single part of that factory, are you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I can't. But I can say that where -- I can tell you about where I worked. It is a relatively small town, and as we say, everything is known in a small town, that word travels fast. So it was not the practice, it wasn't what you were describing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do you say to the possibility that in one of the factories, the Sintevit company, there was a requirement for people to, as it were, sign up to the HVO and that they'd lose their jobs or be put on standby if they did not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I'm hearing this for the first time from you. For me that is absurd. I did not hear of that happening. If that did happen, it was incognito but officially, no, quite certainly, quite definitely but it's absurd that anyone would sign anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can just go briefly into private session then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To make sure I understand your evidence about the factory or the factories, finished weapons were being produced within Vitez even if not in a single factory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: No. The finished products, I'm speaking in general, I'm not speaking about 1993 and the end of 1992, the product that we produced went to where it was finished, and the finishing took place, 90 per cent of the cases, in Pretis, Vogosce; Krusik in Valjevo, Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Well, can the witness please see Exhibit 1220.2, and if we go first to the cover sheet on the ELMO and then to page 11, we'll have to try and find the matching passages in the B/C/S. If I can have the B/C/S version, I'll find what I want, I think, quite quickly. Sorry, this is proving to be rather more difficult than I expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you'd look at the two pages particularly that the usher will hand you, this is a document prepared in the defence office of Vitez in September of 1993 described as an assessment of military, political, economic and other conditions in wartime. It's a long document, but if the English version is put on the ELMO now at page 11, you, Mr. Bekavac, will find on the page you're looking at in the original, a list of things which begins with 600. Do you find that, 600 rockets for multi-rocket launchers? I think it's at the top of a page.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Just let me have a look at the date, please. Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, if you would be good enough to go to the previous page, because in the original version, this covers two pages. If you go to one page before and about three paragraphs up, you'll see this short paragraph reading as follows in the English: "Wartime production was organised before the conflict with Muslim forces. It was organised illegally because of the presence of Muslim personnel in special purpose production." Can you help us, please, to help us understand that paragraph that it comes in this September 1993 report from the Vitez defence office. Why was wartime production organised illegally because of the presence of Muslim personnel in special purpose production?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I don't think this was true. This isn't correct. Especially if I look at who composed this document. Real wartime production began from the first days. That's what it says if you have the document. When I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. went up there to the war production plant to work with gunpowders, I was given the task of organising wartime production and to find the people to do this, who were capable of working in this field, so this is not correct. So what goals and purposes this was drawn up for I really cannot say but it's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next couple of paragraphs, "Organised wartime production began from the first days of the armed conflict with the Muslim armed forces and was organised by the Vitez municipality defence office in accordance with the directive from the Vitez HVO offices through appointed wartime directors or representatives of the firms." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Wartime production was organised some time at the beginning of May, and I'm talking about myself, wartime production. And the director was at the head of this, and the others working with explosives and I, myself, was in charge of the gunpowder production. So that did not take place immediately after the conflict broke out. Perhaps you have a document which says when I came to do wartime production. And without me, you couldn't organise production.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two more questions, one on this document and one outside it, if that would be convenient before the break. I would hope to finish before the break, but I've just got a few too many questions. If we jump over one paragraph, please, and move to the paragraph that begins with the figures, Mr. Bekavac, we see that it's said that with the production of material and technical supplies well organised, the following was manufactured under the most difficult conditions in two months of production. It sets out 600 rockets, 5.000 shells, and we can see the rest of the figures, including 3.000 kilograms of gunpowder produced for the Republic of Croatia, 1.000 kilograms of gunpowder produced for local needs. Is this description of the war effort correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: When you use the term "wartime conditions", you know, war was all over. There was war going on all over. The BH army was getting ready. The other person was getting ready. There were war conditions and difficult war conditions of war all over the place. And when you speak about these figures, it doesn't say that they were produced. It says they were completed, which means that the metal parts arrived via the mountains, caps came from Gorazde, and they were loaded up onto horses and so on. Because Vitez, at that time, was still conditionally speaking free and this kind of production could be organised. So it just says "completed." It doesn't say "produced," it says "completed" the elements which arrived from roundabout routes from other factories. So that was not actual production.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But is it right that you were producing at such a rate that you could produce 3.000 kilograms of gunpowder to be sent to the Republic of Croatia? You were in charge. Please help us.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: It was produced. Now, whether it went to Croatia at this point in time, I can't say. I don't know where it went. I can't say. That was up to the commercial department. But when you're talking about 3.000 kilograms, do you know that you can produce that amount in Vitez in a single day? We had enormous capacities; we could do one and a half thousand tonnes of gunpowder per year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now for half an hour. Mr. Bekavac, please don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over. Could you be back in half an hour's time, that will be at twenty-five to twelve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From the document we've just been considering, is it clear that the municipal defence office were making the decisions about what should happen with the product of your factories?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I was working in manufacturing, and I received direct orders from the factory management. I was not a politician so I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know enough about the process of distribution and at least delivery of materials to know that in Vitez, and you've told us what a small town it is, staff went from the -- the materials went from the factory and they would have been eventually in the hands of the brigade, the Viteska Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Well, as I say, I was involved in manufacturing. The job of who was to get the finished products was not my job. I do, however, know, and I did see people with insignia because there were signs according to towns, and I saw vehicles in front of the management building, when I went there, with Tuzla licence plates, Sarajevo, Bugojno, Konjic. I've already listed all those, and there were licence plates from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last point on this topic for your assistance, please, is this: Gunpowder, the extremely sensitive material it is, and valuable in time of war, was no doubt kept on terms of considerable security; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: There was the usual security in the factory, in the plant. As for the depot, there was the factory security which took the usual security measures which were always normal, and it was kept under lock and key.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that if somebody wanted 250 kilograms of gunpowder, they'd have to be an accredited purchaser and they'd have to get it in a regular way?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes. That's self-evident.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And certainly one of the people to whom you were supplying, and for whom you were working, was the municipal defence office.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I did not deliver materials to anyone. I was only involved in manufacturing. There was a commercial department in our factory. Everybody's duty was very clear. It was my duty to be in manufacturing. At that time, if I learned something else, that was my own private matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you learn where the gunpowder for the Vitez truck bomb came from?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard --

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I don't know that. I think it was not gunpowder. I think perhaps it was explosive, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard of this truck bomb and how in reality it was an act of terrorism. You must have been alarmed to know that some explosive substance was available for such an act in your town, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I heard the explosion. Of course how they came to obtain the explosive substance, well, there was a state of war so to say, and there were extremists walking about who were not controlled by anyone. So it is not surprising if someone somehow managed to get hold of that substance because, at that moment, everyone was only concerned with staying alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to debate that further. Can the witness please see 544.2, a new exhibit. Just a few documents about weapons and a few other topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, just a technical matter. Your Honour, I'm not sure that we have received earlier a document discussed until now, 1220, the report on the war production.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sure we have because I remember discussing it with another witness. It was one of the outstanding exhibits, and it was produced on an earlier occasion and I'll be able to give detail of when in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That can be dealt with later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It may be that it is under a different number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll check for Mr. Kovacic, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Bekavac, is dated the 15th of March so it's before the major conflict broke out. It's from the same author, Marijan Skopljak, as of the last report, and we can see that it goes to the command of Central Bosnia Operative Zone but also to the SPS and to one other enterprise. It's a request for a written report on the implementation and delivery and distribution of strategic products of special importance for the defence. Just help us, is that phrase, "strategic products of special importance for defence" the normal way in which weapons are described?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes it is food that is most important, although it's a usual thing. But for our products, they were always described as strategic products.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's fine. But what we do see, it says this: "Pursuant to the conclusion of the /?HVO - Croatian Defence Council/ administration of Vitez, we URGENTLY request that you send us a written report on the implementation of all delivery and distribution of strategic products of special importance for defence between 5 March 1993 and 15 March 1993. We also request you tell us who gave permission for which buyer, which item and what quantity ..." Doesn't this reflect quite simply that completed objects of strategic importance, products of strategic importance, were being provided by the SPS factory in March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: We have said that, and it's in the survey, that certain products up to the beginning of 1993, that they were delivered to individual buyers. They were delivered. The question is not sufficiently clear to me. I don't know what you are getting at with this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These are documents that you can interpret better for us than we can for you, and that's why I'm seeking your help. You've been seeking to say to some degree, I thought, that you only provided bits and pieces for final weapons. I'm suggesting to you that this document shows quite clearly that there was widespread and substantial distribution of completed weapons for the HVO in March of 1993, before the conflict broke out. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: No, you are not correct. It has to be said that this was a chemical plant in Vitez. We did not have the kind of machinery and equipment like Novi Travnik, Bratstvo, for example, or Pretis, Vogosce to be able to produce and distribute these. We have said this in different ways. It was assembled, these things were assembled here; although we did not have sufficient professional staff, so it was done by amateurs. But these things were assembled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They were assembled on that same site, the SPS site; have I understood that correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: It's evident in the survey presented by the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Very briefly, 1166.2, please, which is an existing exhibit. This is later in the year, Mr. Bekavac; this is the 16th of August. This is a document that goes from the Croatian Defence Council, Travnik defence administration. It's a request for materiel and technical equipment, and it sends the specifications of what was needed in terms of bullets, machine-guns, and so on. Now, is that the sort of materiel that was being assembled, in whatever amateur fashion, in your factory, please?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: It doesn't mean what you say it means. This is a request at a higher level. But nothing was assembled because bullets are finished. These are rifle bullets. It has nothing to do with assembly, this document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Bekavac. Well, you're here, you see, as the witness who knows all about the factory and factories and that's why I'm seeking your help, so please be patient with me. On what part of Vitez factory territory, if any, would bullets, rifles, and machine-guns be either made or completed?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I don't know everything about the factory, I wish I did, because it was a very large compound. There was the plastics department, the explosives department. And things were not completed, the things you mentioned were not completed in the factory. A rifle is a rifle. Where they kept rifles, I don't know. A rifle is a finished product, so is a bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just this: On this document it says at the end: "After procurement, make materiel available to the Logistics Department of the Command of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone and by no means to individual brigades or municipalities ..." When you were producing gunpowder, in thinking back, was the same approach to distribution taken with your materiels?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: A distinction should be drawn between before the outbreak of the conflict and after. Before the outbreak of the conflict, it was distributed, and there are surveys, it was distributed to everyone all over Bosnia-Herzegovina. After the conflict broke out, we were part of the war effort and we were struggling to defend ourselves and survive in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure that's an answer to the question. If you can't answer the question, I'll move on. But I'll just give you one quick chance. Does this approach to distribution via the logistics department of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, does that, in your recollection, match the distribution of your gunpowder?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I produced gunpowder and we handed it over to the warehouse. There were other people who were in charge of distributing it. And to whom it was delivered after the outbreak of the conflict, I don't know. Of course, we would not have sent it to the army of BH. It would have come back to us like a boomerang.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know why documents of procurement of this kind were sent to the office of Mr. Kordic, as this one was?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I don't know. That's politics at a higher level.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: But everywhere politicians are aware of certain documents, and someone sent this. Perhaps Mr. Kordic asked for it but I can only assume that [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A quick look, please, at 1419.2, which I think relates to the -- it doesn't relate to, it fleshes out -- sorry, 1419.1, my mistake. I produce it having in mind the blank forms and documents of D113/2 this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. I have no objection. I just want to make a correction to the record. I think it's important. On page 41, line 5, the witness said: "Perhaps Mr. Kordic did not ask for it," at least that's what I think. The witness can say whether that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the word "not" is not on the record. That's my assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand the sense of this. "Everywhere politicians are aware of certain documents, and someone sent this." This is the answer on the transcript. "Perhaps Mr. Kordic asked for it but I can only assume that." Now, then, Mr. Bekavac, is that what you said? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: The beginning is all right, and then I said I assume he did not ask for it because it was the custom for politicians, it was the custom from the old system that everything is sent to politicians so they would know about everything. But that's just my assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's just meaningless. That's a perfectly meaningless statement. "Everywhere politicians are aware of certain documents and someone sent this. Perhaps Mr. Kordic asked for it, but I can only assume that." Now, that is an answer which actually makes sense. To say, "Perhaps Mr. Kordic didn't ask for it," doesn't make sense. Are you sure that's what you said originally?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I said that for the simple reason that I personally do not know Mr. Kordic at all, but I know that he was a politician in Central Bosnia and that very often he was on television and so on. And I said that I assume because the Defence counsel asked me whether I knew that Mr. Kordic had got this. And I said I don't know, maybe someone sent it to him without him asking for it, perhaps, but I can only assume that. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 1419.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 24th of April of 1994 from the Travnik defence administration, but it goes to Puljic and it relates to wartime production in the period August 1993 to May 1994. If we turn over the page, for example, to items 30 and onwards, 30 to 38, it sets out details of gunpowder production in kilograms and by gunpowder type. Does this seem to you to relate to the production in which you were engaged in that period?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: It says here "gunpowder." I did take part. Whether these are the exact quantities, I cannot say now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does it look about right to you or not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I can't say with any certainty because it was eight years ago, so I don't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But did you --

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I can't say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have to provide weekly production reports, and did they go to the defence administration? That's what it says at the bottom, that there were weekly production reports, and we can see the heading of the document. Were you reporting to the defence administration on a weekly basis?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the wartime production. After the outbreak of the conflict, I sent reports on production to my immediate superior, the director, who was above me, my superior, and he contacted the administration for wartime production.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last document -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: May I just add something, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: These quantities, we often produced not according to the actual needs, but it was kept in the warehouse. So this is not a reflection of the amounts of final products. These are quantities of how much -- from these quantities, hundreds of thousands of bullets could have been made, thousands and thousands, and because there are some bullets which require very little gunpowder in them, five, six, ten, or twenty grams.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. A very brief look at 1246.1 and then we're done with documents, I think. This is an existing document. We needn't look at all of it. It's dated the 13th of October. It comes from the Vitez command. It's signed by Mario Cerkez and the heading, the first paragraph under the word Warning says: "On the basis of work today in the SPS enterprise, it is clear that the level of production sometimes slumps and is sometimes stable." It sets out difficulties and, in paragraph five, if you just move it up a touch, a little bit further please, thank you very much. It says, "We warn you that you must put an end to personal conflicts and disagreements. This will get us nowhere. Save this for some other time and allow material and human potential to be used in production at the SPS." Do you remember Mr. Cerkez taking this degree of direct involvement in the affairs of the SPS?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: This is just a warning. I don't read this as his direct intervention, because the date here cannot mean that it concerns only the Vitez Brigade. Item five, perhaps it says, "Forget about personal conflicts and disagreements." To me it looks like trying to calm the situation. The production had really declined, and -- but all the output at that time was envisaged for everybody, and part of it went to the BH army. From the date, we can see that it was still so early in January 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Bekavac, I was going to pass from this document, but your answer raises this issue. Although I had identified this document as coming from the Vitez command, I had said nothing whatsoever about its significance for the Vitez Brigade. I simply asked about Mr. Cerkez. Why did you tell us voluntarily in your answer, please, that it cannot mean that it concerns only the Vitez Brigade? Why did you tell us that, please?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I said it because -- well, I saw Mario Cerkez's signature. And your question implied that he had asked for it only for the Vitez Brigade. No. It's a warning that one needs to manufacture and work for Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole. That is both for the BH army and the HVO. That is why I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, my question again was whether he got involved in the affairs of your factory to this degree. And you see references to women engaged in the production process, sheet metal --

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then, how come he's writing this document? This is Mr. Cerkez's signature; how come he's writing this document? Can you explain it, please?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: You know what, this is the first time I see this document and I don't know who wrote it, but I see nothing bad here. The war was raging around us already and Serbs were to come down from Vlasic and enter Vitez any minute. Could I remove my family from there, I would have removed them from Vitez. I don't know. But I'm telling you, it was -- there was a general wartime atmosphere between the BH army and the HVO -- no, there were some tensions, but we were expecting an exodus.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're off the question, Mr. Bekavac. It's a very simple question. If the answer is you don't know how he wrote this document, just say so and we'll move on. Do you know why he came to write this document?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I've already answered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I don't know. The first time I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your holiday house in the few kilometres outside Vitez, you did not hand your house over to the troops for them to use, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: We placed it at the disposal, but my cottage was not used but, regrettably, it was burned down by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It wasn't used by the soldiers in their training?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Soldiers, well, we turned over the keys. I don't think they used mine. They did use some others and they did use the mountaineer's lodge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Marko Lujic. You don't know what he was doing on the 16th of April because you were in your basement.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you came out of your basement, you found that your Muslim neighbours had been interned. Why had they been interned?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I did not establish that straight away. It was only later, around 12.00, that I heard that. To my mind, they were interned or taken in correctly, that is what I learned from my neighbour, [redacted], to protect them in the first place. And once the conflict broke out --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Protect them from whom, please? Who was likely to attack them?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I said in Vitez there were a large number of groups uncontrolled who did as they pleased, and were hardly controlled by anyone. It was very easy to come by weapons at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to come to those in a minute. Just so I can follow the logic of your answer, you are telling us, are you, that these Muslims were all imprisoned or interned to protect them from these other groups. That's your evidence, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes. First and foremost, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And where is your evidence for that, please? I mean, where did you get that idea or was it just an idea?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: That's my idea. But the practice showed also that even before the conflict, there were all sorts of groups. There were robberies, plunders, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And whose decision was it to intern these Muslims so they could be saved from the Herzegovinians?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: It wasn't Herzegovinians at the time. They were not there. The Herzegovinians were there before the conflict, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which were the groups from whom they had to be protected on the 16th of April, then, so that we can understand it? Give us the names of the groups.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know the exact names. But there were all sorts of groups which were not registered anywhere, which were armed and which stayed behind after the retreat of Croats from the area of Jajce and other municipalities up there. I did not know them. But there were quite a lot of weapons around and it was very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it had been dangerous for some time in your area. Were the Muslims given the choice of this protection? Were they told, "Well, we'll take you into custody if you'd like to be protected from these other groups. But of course because you're people of full age, you're entitled to stay at home if you wish"? Were they told that, or were they just imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I don't know what they were told. But the situation before the conflict was not like that. The Muslims were rather safe. "Rather," I say. Pretty safe. I won't say that there were not some excesses; I mean, they keep occurring here and there. But when that situation happened, someone - and I don't know who - might have decided to put them up there because there, they were safe. As I said today, in that shelter, in that room, nobody missed a hair from his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Bekavac, your account is, and you know it, absolute nonsense. This was the last stages in the takeover, and it coincided with an attack on the Muslims by the Croats of Vitez; that's correct, isn't it? It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: No. That's what you say, but that is not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell me, then, this: Was it Darko Kraljevic and the Vitezovi who imprisoned the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask for a closed session on that question; the witness otherwise cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last question is this: What about the threats that were made to blow up the SPS factory if the Muslims proceeded with their advance on Vitez? Do you remember anything about that, please?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Well, I remember it. You could read it in the press, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These were --

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: No, not our press, because we did not have it at the time. But the Croatian press and the TV and some foreign newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let there be no doubt about it. These were serious threats, weren't they, to blow up that factory, or was it all just propaganda? It was your factory; you should know.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: No, no, no. It was a desperate attempt to save people who had spent a year in a complete encirclement in a ghetto.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll be quite short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Bekavac, perhaps just one question to support some of your theses that you explained to us. You mentioned those uncontrolled groups of individuals or soldiers. Tell us one thing, please: Is it true that your own brother was abducted by one such group?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I am very happy, because we met only once and you never raised this, but I'm very happy that I am able to give this answer to the Honourable Court. On the eve of the conflict, at the time of the village guards, my brother was below my house on his guard duty at 9.30, and Muslims from the village of Vranjska came up, or rather to be more precise, from the hamlet of Pezici. They captured my brother, took him up there. He spent two days up there. They beat him; he was battered very badly. The hamlet of Pezici is very high; it's between Busovaca and Vitez. They were given samples of cigarettes or food or something to take up the hill, and they kept firing bullets at their feet or, rather, next to their feet, to frighten them. He almost died of fear on the road. After that, the whole of Rijeka, practically the whole of Vitez, rose, requesting that he be released. When they realised that they had all risen in protest and that that did not bode well, then they released him. He was badly bruised. And I remember that his return was also taped on a private TV camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that the whole place rose up in protest. Was your brother a well-known person in the place?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a well-known athlete, and he also taught at school. Once upon a time he was Bosnia-Herzegovina's table tennis champion, so that he was a well-known figure there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. A question about the Sintevit and attempts to represent things in a different light. In the beginning, the Prosecutor asked you if those statements which you say were not signed in your part of the company were perhaps signed at the Sintevit. Tell us, do you remember, who was the Sintevit manager at that time, in those months immediately preceding the conflict, in 1992, beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: 1993, I can't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But if I mentioned the name of Alija Basic, would that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, Alija Basic from Travnik. Yes, you're quite right. An engineer, an applied chemist. Yes, he was from Travnik; he lived in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know, what was he by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: And I mean an orthodox Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you think that he was firing Muslims in order to secure his position?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Well, that cannot be excluded. But he was very close with the SDA. As far as I know, he was highly involved in politics at the time so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And he nevertheless remained in the Vitezit all the time.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. In the Sintevit.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, at the Sintevit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: A lot was said here about the report about the wartime production; I think it is Z1220.2. Just one detail. I believe the rest is clear. You said that you joined the wartime -- that you started wartime production sometime in early May 1993. When you came to the factory one of those days, was Marko Lujic's team already there? Were he and his team already there?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, they were already there. Now, what their task was. But all it came down to was the preparation of the production.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
