utterances.text: Thank you. The term "wartime conditions" was interpreted in a different manner. So let me ask you this: Do you remember when was there an attempt to bomb it, and when did the Yugoslav People's Army try to overfly the place in 1992? Could you tell us, roughly?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I think it was -- I believe -- I think it was 1993. It wasn't wintertime so it must have been summer. Spring/summer perhaps, very roughly. I wouldn't know the date. I can't be more specific than that. But I know that it was not wintertime, because I remember that I was in front of my house at the time. That is how I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But are you quite sure that it was one year before the Muslim-Croat conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Since then was it that the wartime production conditions were introduced in the plant?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And those wartime production --

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes, they were introduced one by one. One cannot say that the wartime production started straight away. But the situation, the circumstances, simply necessitated the gradual transition to wartime production. The term "wartime production" is used, but actually what it means is just slightly stricter control, and so on. But roughly that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify the term once and for all. In early 1993, that is, a couple of months before the conflict between the BH army and the HVO, the production conditions, were they perceived as normal or as special conditions, perhaps even wartime conditions?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: As for the production itself, it is always the same, but there are stricter measures of safety, of precaution, that is, the production unfolded normally but the circumstances told us that we needed to be more cautious, so there were more guards around the plant and so on. This is such a sensitive, such a vulnerable factory that, you know, with a very slight effort, one can cause a proper disaster.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, we understand that. Thank you. When you looked at those reports about the amounts of quantities of various products put out, you mentioned the figure and I should like to ask you about it something. Can you tell us, under normal production conditions, for instance, in earlier years, in the '80s, what was the annual output of gunpowder?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: The factory could put out almost one and a half thousand tonnes per day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Per day you mean or per year?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: No, per year. I said 1.5 thousand tonnes per annum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. And under wartime conditions, do you think that they could put out the same quantity?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Oh, no, absolutely not, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think there was a misunderstanding between you and the -- my learned friend. Let us try to clarify that point. You told us in the beginning of your testimony today that the plant management pursued the policy which you called the policy, that is, political parties, political relations between people would never cross the threshold of the plant. However, after the 16th of April, 1993, when the conflict broke out, the plant was not run by its earlier management, was it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you told us in your testimony that then the wartime production was organised by the municipal HVO defence office, and subsequently the administration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it was no longer the management and the company was no longer independent; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And from those same reports, in one of those documents, you saw mentioned bullets, rifles, and so on and so forth. Will you please answer only yes or no, but did anyone ever, at the SPS, at that place, make a single rifle?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: No, that was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Anywhere, any time, did anyone make a single other piece of weapon, a mortar or anything like that at that place at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: No - you can be a hand-held thrower [as interpreted] or whatever. That is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What about bullets?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: No, that is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bekavac, is it right that the weapons that you manufactured during the war, that is in the latter half of 1993, meant different devices, different mines which were designed there at that time and hitherto unknown as a military product?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Absolutely true. We used the railway carriage axles to make mines. We simply had to do it. We were encircled, and we had to defend ourselves so that we used railway carriage axles which are made of very high-grade steel. That is what we used on our lathes, our workers improvised it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the key word was "improvisation," wasn't it, Mr. Bekavac?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bekavac, just one more thing. One of these documents that was shown you, Z1419.1, since this was shown you, I may as well ask. We have the head of the service for planning and monitoring, Filip Filipovic. We have his signature on the left-hand side. Is it a common procedure that these services submit such reports on the quantities manufactured and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And this Filip Filipovic, is that that soldier, that HVO colonel? Wasn't he regional commander? Is that him? Is that him or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I think that's him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Military.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, the military. Filip Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the other one is an engineer.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: No, no. This one is engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, it says Filip Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: No. No. That's not the one. That's not the man from the army. No, this was the planning and analytical department. Yes, he is an engineer, and he was the head of the department for planning and analysis for materiel. You got me confused because I knew that that colonel, at that time, was quite a well-known figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that was just a slip.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And on the right-hand side, there was a signature, I don't know if you saw it.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: I never even read that page. Could you please show it to me or will you read it to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, then I'll ask you. Will you agree with me -- yes, now you are being shown the document. Will you agree with me that at that time, the signature that figures on the right-hand side comes from a man who did hold that post, head of the wartime production sector. Look at the date of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR BEKAVAC
utterances.text: 26th of April, 1994, yes, yes. 26th of April, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Bekavac, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. It is now concluded. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, it may be that we could use a few minutes usefully considering the rest of your case. I have now your list of witnesses dated the 12th of September for next week. I notice that you listed 11, but one of them has already given evidence so we're down to 10. Now, have you some replacements?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we noticed that error I think day before yesterday. And partially out of that at least a group which is coming. Indeed a group is coming this evening, about half of them, and on Tuesday next week about other half and we are, of course, adding two persons more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That will be 12 witnesses next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Hopefully, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have also in front of me your list of the 31st of August which lists a total of 66 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are, according to the schedule which we have provided, 22 days left for your case. Now, are you in a position to update us about the number of witnesses you propose to call? We notice, in particular, that you have only provided two affidavits to date. It would seem that a number of these witnesses who are being called at the moment would be appropriate candidates for affidavit evidence, and it may be that you should be looking at that rather than bringing them here to give evidence live. Now, can you update us on the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Certainly. First of all, I would like to tell you that we are scheduling a meeting this afternoon of our team to reconsider and analyse how we did so far and what is else absolutely needed for remaining time, or maybe just as to keep it on the list as contingency, shall I say. However, I may now just briefly tell you what is our impression, but if you want, I can brief you on that status in detail on Monday, I guess, is our first trial day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What can you tell us about the affidavits?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Generally two things. First, the affidavits. We were working on that a lot, but the problem is basically, Your Honour, that we do not have, at least as a general rule, two persons talking about the same event except some circumstances which are more or less of general knowledge, should I say. So if we bring one on the particular event, we don't think we need a second witness on the same event. We may add or not add affidavit, but that will not change the time, I mean the progress of the witnesses. We do have some witnesses already -- some affidavits prepared, but we are not yet sure to which witness we can attach that story. So if it is important testimony, we are bringing that witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if it is another village witness, it may well be -- of course, I'm just speaking for myself -- but it may well be that the witness can be generally corroborative as opposed to corroborative of a particular piece of evidence. You should look at the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you, of course, notice at least so far never had two witnesses for the same village. But that is one of the restrictions logically. But nevertheless, the number which I also could just inform about, how does it look generally to us, the last list we informed about the Chamber was 65 witnesses, roughly. Some of them are kind of contingency. If particular witness listed before that is not able or whatever, sick or whatever, then I can introduce other one as alternative. That was done more or less on contingency basis in order to avoid any argument on whether this witness, particular witness who may not come, was earlier given on the list to the other side. So I guess that we will be able to finish our case somewhere around maybe 50 or so witnesses, perhaps, anywhere less than 55, but that is exactly the job we are trying to do this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Perhaps you'd bear in mind that it's quite clear that your case is going much more quickly than anticipated. The witnesses have been going this week much more quickly. Cross-examination has been succinct and, therefore, if you would plan to have an excess of witnesses here, we may be able to get through the whole thing much more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is exactly one of the reasons why we decided to analyse the situation this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll hear the results of that on Monday, bearing in mind that we wish to remain on schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Certainly that is always -- we never considered to change the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll sit again on Monday at half past nine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
